Concept C01 — What is a differential equation?

You already know that a derivative tells us how fast something changes. If a graph is y=y(x)y=y(x)y=y(x), then

y′=dydx=slope of the tangent at (x,y).y'=\frac{dy}{dx}=\text{slope of the tangent at }(x,y).y′=dxdy​=slope of the tangent at (x,y).

For example, y′=2xy'=2xy′=2x says: at horizontal position xxx, the graph must have slope 2x2x2x. At x=1x=1x=1 the slope must be 2. At x=0x=0x=0 it must be 0. It does not give the height of the graph yet.

All curves y=x2+Cy=x^2+Cy=x2+C have derivative 2x2x2x. Changing the constant CCC moves the graph up or down without changing its slope at a given xxx.

y′=2x⟹y=x2+C.y(0)=1⟹C=1.y'=2x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad y=x^2+C. \qquad y(0)=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad C=1.y′=2x⟹y=x2+C.y(0)=1⟹C=1.

A differential equation contains an unknown function and one or more of its derivatives. To solve it, find the function or family of functions that obeys it. A general solution keeps arbitrary constants. A particular solution uses extra information, such as y(0)=1y(0)=1y(0)=1, to fix them. That extra information is an initial condition: it gives a starting point or a starting slope.

Quick check: differentiate your answer and substitute into the original equation. Also check the initial condition. Checking only the final numerical value can miss a wrong curve.

Concept C02 — Order and degree: use two separate questions

Order: which is the highest derivative present?

y′ is first order,y′′ is second order,y′′′ is third order.y' \text{ is first order},\qquad y'' \text{ is second order},\qquad y''' \text{ is third order}.y′ is first order,y′′ is second order,y′′′ is third order.

Degree: after the equation is written as a polynomial in its derivatives, what is the power of the highest-order derivative? Lower derivatives may have larger powers; those powers do not decide the degree.

(y′′′)2+(y′′)3+y′+y4=0⟹order=3,degree=2.(y''')^2+(y'')^3+y'+y^4=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{order}=3,\quad \text{degree}=2.(y′′′)2+(y′′)3+y′+y4=0⟹order=3,degree=2.

Here y4y^4y4 does not affect either answer: it is the function, not a derivative.

Radicals: remove derivative radicals algebraically when possible.

1+(y′)2=y′′⟹1+(y′)2=(y′′)2.\sqrt{1+(y')^2}=y'' \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 1+(y')^2=(y'')^2.1+(y′)2​=y′′⟹1+(y′)2=(y′′)2.

Order 2, degree 2. The original equation also requires y′′≥0y''\ge0y′′≥0. Squaring helps classify the equation but can introduce extra candidate solutions; check the original sign if you solve it.

Degree may not exist.

y′′+sin⁡(y′′)+y=0:order=2,degree is undefined.y''+\sin(y'')+y=0: \qquad \text{order}=2,\quad\text{degree is undefined}.y′′+sin(y′′)+y=0:order=2,degree is undefined.

The derivative is inside sine, so we cannot turn this into a polynomial in derivatives by algebraic removal of radicals or denominators. By contrast, sin⁡x\sin xsinx or exe^xex as a coefficient is fine: y′′+sin⁡x y′=0y''+\sin x\,y'=0y′′+sinxy′=0 has degree 1.

Important for JEE Main: do not answer “degree 3” merely because you see (y′)3(y')^3(y′)3. First circle the highest derivative, then inspect its power.

Concept C03 — Form an equation by removing arbitrary constants

An arbitrary constant labels different members of a family. Differentiation often removes it. Example:

y=Cx2⟹y′=2Cx.xy′=2y.y=Cx^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad y'=2Cx. \qquad xy'=2y.y=Cx2⟹y′=2Cx.xy′=2y.

We multiplied by xxx and used Cx2=yCx^2=yCx2=y. The final equation contains no CCC.

For a regular family with nnn independent constants, eliminating them usually gives an equation of order nnn. Count independent combinations, not names:

y=(c1+c2)x⟹y=Ax.y=(c_1+c_2)x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad y=Ax.y=(c1​+c2​)x⟹y=Ax.

There is only one free coefficient AAA. Similarly,

Rcos⁡(x+ϕ)=Rcos⁡ϕcos⁡x−Rsin⁡ϕsin⁡x=Acos⁡x+Bsin⁡x.R\cos(x+\phi)=R\cos\phi\cos x-R\sin\phi\sin x =A\cos x+B\sin x.Rcos(x+ϕ)=Rcosϕcosx−Rsinϕsinx=Acosx+Bsinx.

Amplitude and phase together represent two independent real coefficients. We use this in Q3. The family-formation questions here use differentiation and elimination; we do not need a full course on solving second-order equations.

Geometry clue: identify the family first. A circle through the origin, a sideways parabola and a vertical parabola need different equations. Draw the family before differentiating if its orientation matters.

Concept C04 — Separation of variables means put each variable on its own side

Suppose

dydx=g(x)h(y).\frac{dy}{dx}=g(x)h(y).dxdy​=g(x)h(y).

The xxx part and the yyy part are multiplied. On a branch where h(y)≠0h(y)\ne0h(y)=0,

dyh(y)=g(x) dx,∫dyh(y)=∫g(x) dx+C.\frac{dy}{h(y)}=g(x)\,dx, \qquad \int\frac{dy}{h(y)}=\int g(x)\,dx+C.h(y)dy​=g(x)dx,∫h(y)dy​=∫g(x)dx+C.

We are using the chain rule in reverse. If H′(y)=1/h(y)H'(y)=1/h(y)H′(y)=1/h(y), then ddxH(y(x))=y′/h(y)\frac d{dx}H(y(x))=y'/h(y)dxd​H(y(x))=y′/h(y).

Example:

y′=2xy⟹dyy=2x dx⟹ln⁡∣y∣=x2+C⟹y=Kex2.y'=2xy \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{dy}{y}=2x\,dx \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \ln|y|=x^2+C \quad\Longrightarrow\quad y=Ke^{x^2}.y′=2xy⟹ydy​=2xdx⟹ln∣y∣=x2+C⟹y=Kex2.

We divided by yyy, so check y=0y=0y=0 separately. It satisfies the original equation and is included when K=0K=0K=0 in the final expression.

Do not force separation on sums. In y′+y=xy'+y=xy′+y=x, writing dy=(x−y)dxdy=(x-y)dxdy=(x−y)dx does not separate anything: the right side still mixes xxx and yyy. Use the linear method in C05.

Useful integrals, with real domains understood:

∫duu=ln⁡∣u∣+C,∫du1+u2=tan⁡−1u+C,∫eu du=eu+C.\int\frac{du}{u}=\ln|u|+C,\qquad \int\frac{du}{1+u^2}=\tan^{-1}u+C, \qquad \int e^u\,du=e^u+C.∫udu​=ln∣u∣+C,∫1+u2du​=tan−1u+C,∫eudu=eu+C.

Here tan⁡−1u\tan^{-1}utan−1u means inverse tangent, not 1/tan⁡u1/\tan u1/tanu. All trigonometric calculus uses radians.

An initial value can save work: instead of introducing a constant and finding it later, use

∫y0y(x)duh(u)=∫x0xg(t) dt,\int_{y_0}^{y(x)}\frac{du}{h(u)} =\int_{x_0}^x g(t)\,dt,∫y0​y(x)​h(u)du​=∫x0​x​g(t)dt,

provided the same valid branch connects the endpoints.

Concept C05 — Linear equations: make a product derivative

A first-order equation is linear in yyy when it has the form

y′+P(x)y=Q(x).y'+P(x)y=Q(x).y′+P(x)y=Q(x).

The unknown yyy and its derivative occur to the first power, and the coefficients depend only on xxx. A y2y^2y2, yy′yy'yy′ or sin⁡y\sin ysiny term makes this form nonlinear.

First make the coefficient of y′y'y′ equal to 1. If a(x)y′+b(x)y=c(x)a(x)y'+b(x)y=c(x)a(x)y′+b(x)y=c(x), divide by a(x)a(x)a(x) on an interval where a(x)≠0a(x)\ne0a(x)=0. Then P=b/aP=b/aP=b/a.

Why do we multiply by an integrating factor? The product rule says

(μy)′=μy′+μ′y.(\mu y)'=\mu y'+\mu' y.(μy)′=μy′+μ′y.

We want the left side of the equation, after multiplication by μ\muμ, to look exactly like this. So choose μ′=μP\mu'=\mu Pμ′=μP. Separating this small equation gives

μ(x)=e∫P(x) dx,(μy)′=μQ,μy=∫μQ dx+C.\boxed{\mu(x)=e^{\int P(x)\,dx}}, \qquad (\mu y)'=\mu Q, \qquad \boxed{\mu y=\int\mu Q\,dx+C}.μ(x)=e∫P(x)dx​,(μy)′=μQ,μy=∫μQdx+C​.

The integrating factor is the multiplier μ\muμ that joins two terms into one product derivative. We normally omit its arbitrary nonzero constant because multiplying the whole equation by a constant changes no solutions.

Notice the pattern!

y′+2xy=x⟹μ=x2x2y′+2xy=x3⟹(x2y)′=x3.y'+\frac2x y=x \quad\overset{\mu=x^2}{\Longrightarrow}\quad x^2y'+2xy=x^3 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad (x^2y)'=x^3.y′+x2​y=x⟹μ=x2​x2y′+2xy=x3⟹(x2y)′=x3.

The factor x2x^2x2 is useful because its derivative is 2x2x2x. That is the reason for the method, not just a formula to memorize.

Coefficient P(x)P(x)P(x) A convenient integrating factor Valid interval
aaa constant eaxe^{ax}eax any interval
n/xn/xn/x xnx^nxn when this is real and nonzero; otherwise use enln⁡∣x∣e^{n\ln|x|}enln∣x∣ avoid x=0x=0x=0
tan⁡x\tan xtanx sec⁡x\sec xsecx up to a nonzero constant on each interval avoid cos⁡x=0\cos x=0cosx=0
2x/(1+x2)2x/(1+x^2)2x/(1+x2) 1+x21+x^21+x2 all real xxx

Important for JEE Main: normalization, the product rule and the initial condition are three separate steps. Check all three. If the product is already visible, use it directly; you need not recompute an integrating factor.

Concept C06 — Homogeneous first-order equations: see a ratio

In this method, “homogeneous” means that the slope depends only on y/xy/xy/x:

y′=F(y/x),x≠0.y'=F(y/x),\qquad x\ne0.y′=F(y/x),x=0.

An equivalent test is unchanged slope under common scaling:

f(λx,λy)=f(x,y)f(\lambda x,\lambda y)=f(x,y)f(λx,λy)=f(x,y)

whenever both points belong to the domain. For a ratio of polynomials, equal total degrees in numerator and denominator often make this happen.

Example:

x2+y2xy=xy+yx=1v+v,v=yx.\frac{x^2+y^2}{xy} =\frac{x}{y}+\frac yx =\frac1v+v,\qquad v=\frac yx.xyx2+y2​=yx​+xy​=v1​+v,v=xy​.

So replace the repeated ratio by vvv:

y=vx,y′=v+xv′.\boxed{y=vx,\qquad y'=v+xv'}.y=vx,y′=v+xv′​.

Why the extra xv′xv'xv′? The ratio vvv usually changes as xxx changes. Differentiate vxvxvx by the product rule. Treating vvv as constant would incorrectly force every solution to be a straight line.

v+xv′=F(v)⟹dvF(v)−v=dxx.v+xv'=F(v) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{dv}{F(v)-v}=\frac{dx}{x}.v+xv′=F(v)⟹F(v)−vdv​=xdx​.

Now it is separable. Before dividing, check roots of F(v)−v=0F(v)-v=0F(v)−v=0: they give possible straight-line solutions y=v0xy=v_0xy=v0​x.

Two uses of the same word: a linear homogeneous equation means y′+P(x)y=0y'+P(x)y=0y′+P(x)y=0, with zero right side. That meaning is different from the ratio method here. Decide from the actual equation.

Concept C07 — Sometimes x is the easier unknown

An equation may be nonlinear in y(x)y(x)y(x) but linear in x(y)x(y)x(y). If inversion is valid locally,

dxdy=1dy/dx.\frac{dx}{dy}=\frac1{dy/dx}.dydx​=dy/dx1​.

Example:

y′=1x+y⟹dxdy=x+y.y'=\frac1{x+y} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{dx}{dy}=x+y.y′=x+y1​⟹dydx​=x+y.

Now write dxdy−x=y\frac{dx}{dy}-x=ydydx​−x=y. This is linear: the unknown is xxx, the independent variable is yyy, and the integrating factor is e−ye^{-y}e−y. The same product-rule logic works.

When to try this: a complicated denominator containing xxx linearly, or a form such as (x+g(y))y′=h(y)(x+g(y))y'=h(y)(x+g(y))y′=h(y). Do not invert through a zero slope, and do not forget restrictions in the original equation. The final relation may describe curves with vertical tangents, where a differentiable y(x)y(x)y(x) branch stops.

Concept C08 — A substitution should simplify the troublesome pattern

Do not choose a new letter randomly. Look at what its derivative would be.

y′/y−1/xy'/y-1/xy′/y−1/x w=ln⁡(y/x)w=\ln(y/x)w=ln(y/x) for positive ratio w′=y′/y−1/xw'=y'/y-1/xw′=y′/y−1/x
xy′−yxy'-yxy′−y with x≠0x\ne0x=0 v=y/xv=y/xv=y/x v′=(xy′−y)/x2v'=(xy'-y)/x^2v′=(xy′−y)/x2
xy′−yxy'-yxy′−y divided by x2+y2x^2+y^2x2+y2 θ=tan⁡−1(y/x)\theta=\tan^{-1}(y/x)θ=tan−1(y/x) θ′=(xy′−y)/(x2+y2)\theta'=(xy'-y)/(x^2+y^2)θ′=(xy′−y)/(x2+y2)

The ratio and inverse-tangent identities are important recognition tools for JEE Main. Derive them once from quotient and chain rules so the numerator is familiar.

A useful supporting extension — Bernoulli's form:

y′+P(x)y=Q(x)yn,n≠0,1.y'+P(x)y=Q(x)y^n,\qquad n\ne0,1.y′+P(x)y=Q(x)yn,n=0,1.

The direct linear formula does not apply because of yny^nyn. On a suitable nonzero real branch, divide by yny^nyn and set

u=y1−n,u′=(1−n)y−ny′.u=y^{1-n},\qquad u'=(1-n)y^{-n}y'.u=y1−n,u′=(1−n)y−ny′.

Then

u′+(1−n)P(x)u=(1−n)Q(x).\boxed{u'+(1-n)P(x)u=(1-n)Q(x)}.u′+(1−n)P(x)u=(1−n)Q(x)​.

It has become linear. For n=2n=2n=2, u=1/yu=1/yu=1/y is especially useful in Q12 and Q31. Check y=0y=0y=0 directly if the original equation allows it. It cannot appear while 1/y1/y1/y is being used.

Concept C09 — Recognize a total differential; exactness is a check for it

You know the product rule:

d(xy)=y dx+x dy.d(xy)=y\,dx+x\,dy.d(xy)=ydx+xdy.

You also know

d ⁣(x2+y22)=x dx+y dy.d\!\left(\frac{x^2+y^2}{2}\right)=x\,dx+y\,dy.d(2x2+y2​)=xdx+ydy.

Thus x dy+y dx=0x\,dy+y\,dx=0xdy+ydx=0 means d(xy)=0d(xy)=0d(xy)=0, so xy=Cxy=Cxy=C. We are looking for one quantity that stays constant.

More generally, if

M(x,y) dx+N(x,y) dy=dF(x,y),M(x,y)\,dx+N(x,y)\,dy=dF(x,y),M(x,y)dx+N(x,y)dy=dF(x,y),

then the equation equals zero when F(x,y)=CF(x,y)=CF(x,y)=C. Such an equation is called exact.

To test the smooth polynomial expressions in this PDF, use

∂M∂y=∂N∂x.\boxed{\frac{\partial M}{\partial y}=\frac{\partial N}{\partial x}}.∂y∂M​=∂x∂N​​.

The symbol ∂\partial∂ means “differentiate with respect to this variable while holding the other one fixed.” For example,

M=3x2y2+2xy⟹My=6x2y+2x.M=3x^2y^2+2xy \quad\Longrightarrow\quad M_y=6x^2y+2x.M=3x2y2+2xy⟹My​=6x2y+2x.

This test comes from M=FxM=F_xM=Fx​, N=FyN=F_yN=Fy​ and equality of the mixed derivatives. For our polynomial functions on the plane, it also lets us recover FFF. On domains with holes, a global converse needs extra care; the PDF's polynomial exactness question has no such issue. This is a supporting source method, not a reason to study a full partial-differential-equations course.

Concept C10 — Slope, tangent, normal and orthogonal trajectories

Tangent: the line that gives the curve's direction at a point. Its slope is y′y'y′.

Normal: the line through that point perpendicular to the tangent.

For two finite nonzero perpendicular slopes,

m1m2=−1,m2=−1m1.m_1m_2=-1,\qquad m_2=-\frac1{m_1}.m1​m2​=−1,m2​=−m1​1​.

A horizontal line is perpendicular to a vertical line; the vertical line has no finite slope. Handle these cases with directions or geometry instead of dividing by zero.

Orthogonal trajectories are a new family of curves that crosses the original family at right angles. The right angle is between the two tangents at the crossing point.

Procedure: eliminate the original family's constant to get its slope m(x,y)m(x,y)m(x,y); set the new slope to −1/m(x,y)-1/m(x,y)−1/m(x,y) where meaningful; solve the new differential equation. Check exceptional horizontal or vertical cases geometrically.

Example clue: y=Cx2y=Cx^2y=Cx2 gives original slope 2y/x2y/x2y/x. The new slope must be −x/(2y)-x/(2y)−x/(2y), not just −2y/x-2y/x−2y/x. Negating a slope alone usually does not make a right angle.

If every normal passes through a fixed point, think circle with that point as centre. A radius is normal to a circle. You can prove it without slope fractions: for centre (0,0)(0,0)(0,0), the radius direction (x,y)(x,y)(x,y) is perpendicular to tangent direction (1,y′)(1,y')(1,y′), so

(x,y)⋅(1,y′)=0⟹x+yy′=0⟹x2+y2=C.(x,y)\cdot(1,y')=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x+yy'=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x^2+y^2=C.(x,y)⋅(1,y′)=0⟹x+yy′=0⟹x2+y2=C.

This connects vectors, coordinate geometry and differential equations.

Concept C11 — Rate problems and integral equations

Proportional to the present amount means

N′=kN⟹N(t)=N0ekt.N'=kN \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{N(t)=N_0e^{kt}}.N′=kN⟹N(t)=N0​ekt​.

N0N_0N0​ is the amount at time zero. k>0k>0k>0 gives growth; k<0k<0k<0 gives decay. Equal time gaps multiply the amount by the same factor; they do not add the same amount.

doubling time T:k=ln⁡2T,N(t)=N0 2t/T.\text{doubling time }T:\quad k=\frac{\ln2}{T},\quad N(t)=N_0\,2^{t/T}.doubling time T:k=Tln2​,N(t)=N0​2t/T.

Mixing: amount changes at

rate in−rate out.\boxed{\text{rate in}-\text{rate out}}.rate in−rate out​.

If volume is VVV and salt amount is SSS, a well-mixed outflow has concentration S/VS/VS/V. Multiply concentration by outflow volume per unit time:

salt out per minute=S kgV L q Lmin=qSV kgmin.\text{salt out per minute}= \frac{S\ \mathrm{kg}}{V\ \mathrm L}\, q\ \frac{\mathrm L}{\mathrm{min}} =\frac{qS}{V}\ \frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{min}}.salt out per minute=V LS kg​q minL​=VqS​ minkg​.

Pure water brings in zero salt. Equal inflow and outflow keep VVV fixed, but the concentration changes as salt leaves.

Integral equations: the fundamental theorem of calculus says

ddx∫axf(t) dt=f(x)\frac d{dx}\int_a^x f(t)\,dt=f(x)dxd​∫ax​f(t)dt=f(x)

for continuous fff. The letter ttt is a temporary integration variable; it disappears after integration. Differentiate to get an equation for fff, and put x=ax=ax=a in the original relation to obtain an initial value. Finally check the original integral equation, because differentiation can lose a constant condition.

Concept C12 — Higher derivatives and sideways families

If only a higher derivative is given, integrate repeatedly:

y′′=g(x)⟹y′=∫g(x) dx+C1⟹y=∫y′ dx+C2.y''=g(x) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad y'=\int g(x)\,dx+C_1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad y=\int y'\,dx+C_2.y′′=g(x)⟹y′=∫g(x)dx+C1​⟹y=∫y′dx+C2​.

Two conditions are needed to determine two independent constants.

For forming an equation of a geometrical family, use its actual orientation:

axis parallel to x:(y−b)2=4a(x−c), a≠0;x=Ay2+By+C, A≠0.\text{axis parallel to }x:\quad (y-b)^2=4a(x-c),\ a\ne0; \qquad x=Ay^2+By+C,\ A\ne0.axis parallel to x:(y−b)2=4a(x−c), a=0;x=Ay2+By+C, A=0.

Here the parabola opens left or right, not up or down.

There are three independent parameters. Differentiating and eliminating them on regular y(x)y(x)y(x) branches gives

y′y′′′−3(y′′)2=0.y'y'''-3(y'')^2=0.y′y′′′−3(y′′)2=0.

Q35 derives this rather than asking you to memorize it. At a sideways parabola's vertex, dy/dxdy/dxdy/dx is not finite, so this equation describes regular branches away from the vertex.

Concept C13 — A correct answer includes the correct branch

  1. Before division, write what could be zero. Test it in the original equation. A valid constant solution is called an equilibrium solution; a constant ratio can give a straight-line solution.
  2. Before logarithms, check the argument. Use ln⁡∣u∣\ln|u|ln∣u∣ for ∫du/u\int du/u∫du/u; if the original question contains ln⁡x\ln xlnx, it already requires x>0x>0x>0.
  3. After a substitution, return to the original variables. Check both the differential equation and the initial value.
  4. Do not cross a forbidden point. An initial-value solution lives on a connected interval containing its starting point, with no denominator zero, forbidden logarithm or tangent pole inside it.
  5. Keep full precision until the last step. If two decimals are requested, round only at the end.

Examples: y=1/[x(3−x)]y=1/[x(3-x)]y=1/[x(3−x)] has poles at 0,30,30,3; the branch through x=1x=1x=1 lies in (0,3)(0,3)(0,3). And y=tan⁡(x2/2)y=\tan(x^2/2)y=tan(x2/2) through (0,0)(0,0)(0,0) stops at the nearest poles x=±πx=\pm\sqrt\pix=±π​, even though tangent is defined again farther away.

Final exam habit: name the pattern before calculating. If direct substitution leaves the unknown function inside an integral, that route has not solved the equation. Try a product derivative, ratio, inverse variable or a useful power instead.

Worked solutions to the 35 PDF questions

Read the question first. Notice the pattern, choose a route, then calculate. Alternative methods below are fully visible.

Question 1 — Order and degree ask two different things

PDF page 75 | MCQ | Notes: C02

The order and degree, respectively, of the differential equation [1+(dydx)2]3/2=kd2ydx2\left[1+\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^2\right]^{3/2}=k\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}[1+(dxdy​)2]3/2=kdx2d2y​ are

  • (a) 2 and 3/2
  • (b) 1 and 2
  • (c) 2 and 2
  • (d) 2 and 3

Notice two different tasks. The highest derivative is y′′y''y′′, so the order is 2. The exponent 3/23/23/2 belongs to a bracket containing y′y'y′. It does not directly give the degree.

For the intended nonzero parameter kkk, square to remove the derivative radical:

[1+(y′)2]3=k2(y′′)2.\left[1+(y')^2\right]^3=k^2(y'')^2.[1+(y′)2]3=k2(y′′)2.

This is polynomial in the derivatives. The highest derivative, y′′y''y′′, has power 2.

order=2,degree=2;option (c).\boxed{\text{order}=2,\quad\text{degree}=2;\quad\text{option (c)}}.order=2,degree=2;option (c)​.

Check the tempting answer: expanding the left bracket would produce (y′)6(y')^6(y′)6, but that is a lower derivative. It cannot decide the degree.

A small condition: squaring can add candidates. A real solution of the original equation must have ky′′>0k y''>0ky′′>0, since [1+(y′)2]3/2>0[1+(y')^2]^{3/2}>0[1+(y′)2]3/2>0. If k=0k=0k=0, the original equation has no real solutions; the stated classification uses the intended nonzero kkk.

Question 2 — Remove constants by matching the same exponential terms

PDF page 75 | MCQ | Notes: C03,C12

The differential equation representing the family y=Ae2x+Be−xy=Ae^{2x}+Be^{-x}y=Ae2x+Be−x, where A,BA,BA,B are arbitrary constants, is

  • (a) y′′−y′−2y=0y''-y'-2y=0y′′−y′−2y=0
  • (b) y′′+y′−2y=0y''+y'-2y=0y′′+y′−2y=0
  • (c) y′′−y′+2y=0y''-y'+2y=0y′′−y′+2y=0
  • (d) y′′−2y′−y=0y''-2y'-y=0y′′−2y′−y=0

Did you notice the two exponential rates, 2 and −1-1−1? Differentiating preserves each exponential and only changes its coefficient. We can remove A,BA,BA,B by combining y,y′,y′′y,y',y''y,y′,y′′.

y=Ae2x+Be−x,y′=2Ae2x−Be−x,y′′=4Ae2x+Be−x.\begin{aligned} y&=Ae^{2x}+Be^{-x},\\ y'&=2Ae^{2x}-Be^{-x},\\ y''&=4Ae^{2x}+Be^{-x}. \end{aligned}yy′y′′​=Ae2x+Be−x,=2Ae2x−Be−x,=4Ae2x+Be−x.​

Look for the combination in the options. In y′′−y′−2yy''-y'-2yy′′−y′−2y, the coefficients are

Ae2x: 4−2−2=0,Be−x: 1−(−1)−2=0.A e^{2x}:\ 4-2-2=0,\qquad B e^{-x}:\ 1-(-1)-2=0.Ae2x: 4−2−2=0,Be−x: 1−(−1)−2=0.

Thus

y′′−y′−2y=0;option (a).\boxed{y''-y'-2y=0;\quad\text{option (a)}}.y′′−y′−2y=0;option (a)​.

Another useful view — quick option check. For an equation y′′+αy′+βy=0y''+\alpha y'+\beta y=0y′′+αy′+βy=0, test each rate rrr in r2+αr+βr^2+\alpha r+\betar2+αr+β. Both r=2r=2r=2 and r=−1r=-1r=−1 must give zero. Option (a) gives r2−r−2=(r−2)(r+1)r^2-r-2=(r-2)(r+1)r2−r−2=(r−2)(r+1). This shortcut follows from the derivatives above; it does not require memorizing a new differential-equation solving method.

Question 3 — Count independent constants, not printed symbols

PDF page 75 | Numerical value | Notes: C03

For the family y=(c1+c2)cos⁡(x+c3)−c4ex+c5y=(c_1+c_2)\cos(x+c_3)-c_4e^{x+c_5}y=(c1​+c2​)cos(x+c3​)−c4​ex+c5​, where c1,c2,c3,c4,c5c_1,c_2,c_3,c_4,c_5c1​,c2​,c3​,c4​,c5​ are arbitrary constants, the order of the differential equation obtained by eliminating the arbitrary constants is ____.

Five symbols do not always mean five independent choices! First join constants that always occur together:

R=c1+c2,D=−c4ec5.R=c_1+c_2,\qquad D=-c_4e^{c_5}.R=c1​+c2​,D=−c4​ec5​.

Then expand the shifted cosine:

y=Rcos⁡(x+c3)+Dex=(Rcos⁡c3)cos⁡x−(Rsin⁡c3)sin⁡x+Dex=Acos⁡x+Bsin⁡x+Dex.\begin{aligned} y&=R\cos(x+c_3)+De^x\\ &=(R\cos c_3)\cos x-(R\sin c_3)\sin x+De^x\\ &=A\cos x+B\sin x+De^x. \end{aligned}y​=Rcos(x+c3​)+Dex=(Rcosc3​)cosx−(Rsinc3​)sinx+Dex=Acosx+Bsinx+Dex.​

There are three independent coefficients, A,B,DA,B,DA,B,D. For example, any pair A,BA,BA,B can be represented by a suitable amplitude and phase.

Check by actually eliminating them.

y′′+y=2Dex.y''+y=2De^x.y′′+y=2Dex.

Differentiate once:

y′′′+y′=2Dex.y'''+y'=2De^x.y′′′+y′=2Dex.

Subtract the previous relation:

y′′′−y′′+y′−y=0.y'''-y''+y'-y=0.y′′′−y′′+y′−y=0.

The highest derivative is third order, and the three functions cos⁡x,sin⁡x,ex\cos x,\sin x,e^xcosx,sinx,ex are independent. Hence

order=3.\boxed{\text{order}=3}.order=3​.

Pattern to keep: simplify sums, products and phase shifts of arbitrary constants before counting them.

Question 4 — Separate the exponential into an x part and a y part

PDF page 75 | MCQ | Notes: C04,C13

If dydx=ex+y\dfrac{dy}{dx}=e^{x+y}dxdy​=ex+y and y(0)=0y(0)=0y(0)=0, then y ⁣(ln⁡32)y\!\left(\ln\dfrac32\right)y(ln23​) equals

  • (a) ln⁡32\ln\dfrac32ln23​
  • (b) ln⁡3\ln3ln3
  • (c) 12ln⁡2\dfrac12\ln221​ln2
  • (d) ln⁡2\ln2ln2

Notice ex+y=exeye^{x+y}=e^x e^yex+y=exey. This is a product of an xxx part and a yyy part. Separation is the short route; directly writing y=∫ex+ydxy=\int e^{x+y}dxy=∫ex+ydx leaves the unknown y(x)y(x)y(x) inside the integral and solves nothing.

e−y dy=ex dx⟹−e−y=ex+C.e^{-y}\,dy=e^x\,dx \quad\Longrightarrow\quad -e^{-y}=e^x+C.e−ydy=exdx⟹−e−y=ex+C.

Use x=0,y=0x=0,y=0x=0,y=0: −1=1+C-1=1+C−1=1+C, so C=−2C=-2C=−2. Therefore

e−y=2−ex,y=−ln⁡(2−ex).e^{-y}=2-e^x,\qquad y=-\ln(2-e^x).e−y=2−ex,y=−ln(2−ex).

The logarithm requires 2−ex>02-e^x>02−ex>0, so the initial branch is x<ln⁡2x<\ln2x<ln2. The requested input ln⁡(3/2)\ln(3/2)ln(3/2) belongs to it.

y ⁣(ln⁡32)=−ln⁡(2−32)=−ln⁡12=ln⁡2;(d).y\!\left(\ln\frac32\right) =-\ln\left(2-\frac32\right) =-\ln\frac12 =\boxed{\ln2;\quad\text{(d)}}.y(ln23​)=−ln(2−23​)=−ln21​=ln2;(d)​.

Check: y′=ex/(2−ex)y'=e^x/(2-e^x)y′=ex/(2−ex) and ex+y=ex/(2−ex)e^{x+y}=e^x/(2-e^x)ex+y=ex/(2−ex) agree; y(0)=0y(0)=0y(0)=0.

Another approach: u=e−yu=e^{-y}u=e−y gives u′=−e−yy′=−exu'=-e^{-y}y'=-e^xu′=−e−yy′=−ex, so u=2−exu=2-e^xu=2−ex directly. It is the same chain-rule idea with a new variable.

Question 5 — A y times y-prime pattern suggests y squared

PDF page 75 | Numerical value | Notes: C05,C06,C08

If dydx=x2+y22xy\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{x^2+y^2}{2xy}dxdy​=2xyx2+y2​, y>0y>0y>0 and y(1)=2y(1)=2y(1)=2, then (y(3))2=(y(3))^2=(y(3))2= ____.

Can you see a derivative hiding after multiplication?

2xyy′=x2+y2.2xyy'=x^2+y^2.2xyy′=x2+y2.

The piece 2yy′2yy'2yy′ is exactly (y2)′(y^2)'(y2)′. Since the question also asks for y(3)2y(3)^2y(3)2, set z=y2z=y^2z=y2. We can solve directly for the quantity we need.

xz′=x2+z⟹z′−zx=x.xz'=x^2+z \quad\Longrightarrow\quad z'-\frac zx=x.xz′=x2+z⟹z′−xz​=x.

For the initial branch x>0x>0x>0, the integrating factor is 1/x1/x1/x:

(zx)′=1,zx=x+C,z=x2+Cx.\left(\frac zx\right)'=1,\qquad \frac zx=x+C,\qquad z=x^2+Cx.(xz​)′=1,xz​=x+C,z=x2+Cx.

z(1)=y(1)2=4z(1)=y(1)^2=4z(1)=y(1)2=4 gives C=3C=3C=3. Thus

y2=x2+3x,y(3)2=9+9=18.y^2=x^2+3x,\qquad \boxed{y(3)^2=9+9=18}.y2=x2+3x,y(3)2=9+9=18​.

The positive solution is y=x2+3xy=\sqrt{x^2+3x}y=x2+3x​ on x>0x>0x>0. Differentiating its square gives 2yy′=2x+32yy'=2x+32yy′=2x+3, which agrees with the original right side after y2=x2+3xy^2=x^2+3xy2=x2+3x is inserted.

Another possible approach — homogeneous ratio.

y=vx,v+xv′=1+v22v,2v dv1−v2=dxx.y=vx,\qquad v+xv'=\frac{1+v^2}{2v}, \qquad \frac{2v\,dv}{1-v^2}=\frac{dx}{x}.y=vx,v+xv′=2v1+v2​,1−v22vdv​=xdx​.

Integration gives −ln⁡∣1−v2∣=ln⁡∣x∣+C-\ln|1-v^2|=\ln|x|+C−ln∣1−v2∣=ln∣x∣+C, hence y2=x2+Kxy^2=x^2+Kxy2=x2+Kx. Dividing by 1−v21-v^21−v2 omits v=±1v=\pm1v=±1, so check y=±xy=\pm xy=±x separately on valid branches. They are the K=0K=0K=0 members. This route works, but z=y2z=y^2z=y2 is shorter here.

Question 6 — The coefficient tan x tells us the integrating factor

PDF page 75 | MCQ | Notes: C05

If dydx+ytan⁡x=sin⁡2x\dfrac{dy}{dx}+y\tan x=\sin2xdxdy​+ytanx=sin2x and y(0)=1y(0)=1y(0)=1, then y(π/3)y(\pi/3)y(π/3) equals

  • (a) 12\dfrac1221​
  • (b) 111
  • (c) 32\dfrac3223​
  • (d) 32−14\dfrac32-\dfrac1423​−41​

Recognize a linear equation: y′+(tan⁡x)y=sin⁡2xy'+(\tan x)y=\sin2xy′+(tanx)y=sin2x. The coefficient of y′y'y′ is already 1. We want a multiplier whose derivative produces the tan⁡x\tan xtanx term.

μ=e∫tan⁡x dx=e−ln⁡∣cos⁡x∣.\mu=e^{\int\tan x\,dx} =e^{-\ln|\cos x|}.μ=e∫tanxdx=e−ln∣cosx∣.

On the interval (−π/2,π/2)(-\pi/2,\pi/2)(−π/2,π/2) containing the initial point, cos⁡x>0\cos x>0cosx>0, so take μ=sec⁡x\mu=\sec xμ=secx.

(ysec⁡x)′=sin⁡2xsec⁡x=2sin⁡x.(y\sec x)'=\sin2x\sec x=2\sin x.(ysecx)′=sin2xsecx=2sinx.

Therefore

ysec⁡x=−2cos⁡x+C,y=Ccos⁡x−2cos⁡2x.y\sec x=-2\cos x+C,\qquad y=C\cos x-2\cos^2x.ysecx=−2cosx+C,y=Ccosx−2cos2x.

y(0)=1y(0)=1y(0)=1 gives C=3C=3C=3. At x=π/3x=\pi/3x=π/3,

y=32−2(12)2=32−12=1;(b).y=\frac32-2\left(\frac12\right)^2 =\frac32-\frac12 =\boxed{1;\quad\text{(b)}}.y=23​−2(21​)2=23​−21​=1;(b)​.

Check without long expansion: the product equation above becomes (ysec⁡x)′=2sin⁡x(y\sec x)'=2\sin x(ysecx)′=2sinx, so multiplication by cos⁡x\cos xcosx gives back the original equation. The target is inside the same interval as 000.

Pattern: sin⁡2x=2sin⁡xcos⁡x\sin2x=2\sin x\cos xsin2x=2sinxcosx makes the integrating-factor integrand simple. Expanding this identity after choosing sec⁡x\sec xsecx exposes the cancellation.

Question 7 — Change which variable is the unknown

PDF page 75 | MCQ | Notes: C07,C13

The general solution of (x+2y3)dydx=y(x+2y^3)\dfrac{dy}{dx}=y(x+2y3)dxdy​=y is

  • (a) x=y3+cyx=y^3+\dfrac cyx=y3+yc​
  • (b) x=y3+cyx=y^3+cyx=y3+cy
  • (c) y=x3+cxy=x^3+cxy=x3+cx
  • (d) x=2y3+cyx=2y^3+cyx=2y3+cy

Why not the usual linear formula in yyy? Solving for y′y'y′ puts x+2y3x+2y^3x+2y3 in the denominator, so the equation is not linear in yyy. But xxx occurs only to the first power. Try making xxx the unknown.

For a nonzero branch,

dxdy=x+2y3y⟹dxdy−xy=2y2.\frac{dx}{dy}=\frac{x+2y^3}{y} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{dx}{dy}-\frac xy=2y^2.dydx​=yx+2y3​⟹dydx​−yx​=2y2.

This is linear in x(y)x(y)x(y). A convenient integrating factor is 1/y1/y1/y on an interval avoiding y=0y=0y=0:

ddy(xy)=2y,xy=y2+C.\frac d{dy}\left(\frac xy\right)=2y, \qquad \frac xy=y^2+C.dyd​(yx​)=2y,yx​=y2+C.

Hence

x=y3+Cy;intended option (b).\boxed{x=y^3+Cy;\quad\text{intended option (b)}}.x=y3+Cy;intended option (b)​.

The division check matters! We divided by yyy. In the original equation, y=0y=0y=0 gives (x+0)⋅0=0(x+0)\cdot0=0(x+0)⋅0=0, so it is a separate valid solution. The implicit family above does not contain the whole line y=0y=0y=0.

Check the family: differentiate x=y3+Cyx=y^3+Cyx=y3+Cy to get 1=(3y2+C)y′1=(3y^2+C)y'1=(3y2+C)y′. Also x+2y3=y(3y2+C)x+2y^3=y(3y^2+C)x+2y3=y(3y2+C), so (x+2y3)y′=y(x+2y^3)y'=y(x+2y3)y′=y. This describes regular y(x)y(x)y(x) branches; a vertical tangent cannot be treated as a finite derivative.

Question 8 — Three doubling periods are easier than finding the rate

PDF page 75 | Numerical value | Notes: C11

The population of a town increases at a rate proportional to its population. It doubles in 444 years. If the population after 121212 years is 100010001000, then the initial population is ____.

What does “rate proportional to population” mean? If the present population doubles, its rate of growth also doubles. It means P′=kPP'=kPP′=kP, not constant growth.

P(t)=P0ekt,P(4)=2P0⟹e4k=2.P(t)=P_0e^{kt},\qquad P(4)=2P_0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad e^{4k}=2.P(t)=P0​ekt,P(4)=2P0​⟹e4k=2.

We do not need a decimal value of kkk. Twelve years contain exactly three 4-year periods:

P(12)=P0(e4k)3=8P0=1000.P(12)=P_0(e^{4k})^3=8P_0=1000.P(12)=P0​(e4k)3=8P0​=1000. P0=10008=125.\boxed{P_0=\frac{1000}{8}=125}.P0​=81000​=125​.

Why adding a fixed number is wrong: the increase from 125 to 250 is 125, while the next increase from 250 to 500 is 250. Equal time gaps multiply by 2; they do not add the same number.

Another compact expression: P(t)=P0 2t/4P(t)=P_0\,2^{t/4}P(t)=P0​2t/4. It directly displays the doubling time. Checking at t=12t=12t=12 gives 125⋅23=1000125\cdot2^3=1000125⋅23=1000.

Question 9 — Perpendicular curves have perpendicular tangents

PDF page 76 | MCQ | Notes: C10

The orthogonal trajectories of the family y=cx2y=cx^2y=cx2 are

  • (a) 2x2+y2=k2x^2+y^2=k2x2+y2=k
  • (b) x2−2y2=kx^2-2y^2=kx2−2y2=k
  • (c) y=kx2y=\dfrac{k}{x^2}y=x2k​
  • (d) x2+2y2=kx^2+2y^2=kx2+2y2=k

First understand the picture. A new curve must cross each original parabola at a right angle. It is the tangent lines at the crossing that must be perpendicular.

For y=cx2y=cx^2y=cx2,

y′=2cx=2yx.y'=2cx=\frac{2y}{x}.y′=2cx=x2y​.

So at a regular crossing the original tangent slope is 2y/x2y/x2y/x. The new slope must be its negative reciprocal:

dydx=−x2y.\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{x}{2y}.dxdy​=−2yx​.

Separate and integrate:

2y dy=−x dx⟹y2=−x22+C⟹x2+2y2=k;(d).2y\,dy=-x\,dx \quad\Longrightarrow\quad y^2=-\frac{x^2}{2}+C \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{x^2+2y^2=k;\quad\text{(d)}}.2ydy=−xdx⟹y2=−2x2​+C⟹x2+2y2=k;(d)​.

Check: at (1,1)(1,1)(1,1), choose original c=1c=1c=1 and new k=3k=3k=3. Their slopes are 222 and −1/2-1/2−1/2, whose product is −1-1−1. The figure uses equal units so that the right angle is shown honestly.

Why merely changing the sign fails: −2y/x-2y/x−2y/x is generally not perpendicular to 2y/x2y/x2y/x. Their product is −4y2/x2-4y^2/x^2−4y2/x2, which is not always −1-1−1. Horizontal/vertical limiting cases need the geometric tangent test, not division by zero.

Question 10 — Both terms already belong to one product derivative

Question 21 — A second derivative needs two integrations

If d2ydx2=12x2\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=12x^2dx2d2y​=12x2, y(0)=1y(0)=1y(0)=1 and y′(0)=2y'(0)=2y′(0)=2, then y(1)y(1)y(1) equals

y(1)=1−1+2e=0.73575888…⟹0.74.y(1)=1-1+\frac2e=0.73575888\ldots \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{0.74}.y(1)=1−1+e2​=0.73575888…⟹0.74​.

Check: y′=1−2e−xy'=1-2e^{-x}y′=1−2e−x, so y′+y=xy'+y=xy′+y=x. Also y(0)=1y(0)=1y(0)=1.

Another useful view: a simple particular solution is yp=x−1y_p=x-1yp​=x−1, because yp′+yp=1+x−1=xy_p'+y_p=1+x-1=xyp′​+yp​=1+x−1=x. The difference z=y−ypz=y-y_pz=y−yp​ must satisfy z′+z=0z'+z=0z′+z=0, so z=Ce−xz=Ce^{-x}z=Ce−x. Question 34 — Interchanging x and y makes the equation linear

For u≠−1u\ne-1u=−1,

∫uu+1 du=x+C⟹u−ln⁡∣u+1∣=x+C.\int\frac{u}{u+1}\,du=x+C \quad\Longrightarrow\quad u-\ln|u+1|=x+C.∫u+1u​du=x+C⟹u−ln∣u+1∣=x+C.

Since u=x+yu=x+yu=x+y, this rearranges to x+y+1=Keyx+y+1=Ke^yx+y+1=Key. We divided by u+1u+1u+1, so check u=−1u=-1u=−1: it gives the valid line y=−x−1y=-x-1y=−x−1. It is already included in the final family when K=0K=0K=0. The inverse-variable linear route keeps it automatically.
